harbor_p09_001.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_001.text: The grounded barge leaned toward the reed bank, showing a stripe of weed that ought to have remained underwater. Its people stood behind the passenger rail while the licensed rescue boat approached from the safer upstream angle. Yue watched from the receiving landing. Yan Su was aboard the rescue craft with its ordinary pilot and assigned crew. The shore desk gave Yue a bounded task for her twenty-first inquiry half-day: help people state contact preferences after arrival, while trained attendants handled immediate care. Nobody asked her to turn the bank into a cultivation trial.

harbor_p09_002.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_002.text: The barge master reported seventeen passengers and six crew, twenty-three people in all. The rescue craft was rated for eight including its own two operating crew, leaving six places per transfer. Yan would return on the barge after the first inspection, freeing his place for the planned passenger groups. Four crossings could bring everyone off if conditions held. The pilot checked the current and set the stop mark before boarding began. Yue heard the numbers repeated through the shore runner and wrote them on the receiving board without trying to decide the water from a distant view.

harbor_p09_003.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_003.text: The first group included an elderly man, a woman with two children, and two passengers who needed ordinary help walking. A rigger fitted the transfer line while the boat lay in its approved position. The people moved one at a time under the crew's direction. The smallest child refused to release a basket containing a duck. Her mother argued until Yan asked whether the basket could be secured separately within the boat's load rating. It could. The duck arrived on shore indignant, alive, and much louder than any rescued passenger.

harbor_p09_004.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_004.text: An ordinary attendant met the boat and guided people to the dry shelter before asking longer questions. Nobody required a wage document in exchange for a seat or a blanket. The emergency landing arrangement had been authorized through the harbor's existing response duty, with its own stores and personnel. Yue waited until the mother said she was ready to speak. Her name was Wu Lian. She wanted a message sent to her sister at the eastern packing lane, but she did not want strangers deciding where her children must live that night.

harbor_p09_005.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_005.text: Yue recorded the requested contact point and asked whether the message could name the landing. Wu Lian said yes. She wanted her sister to come if she could, not to be told the family had been placed somewhere permanently. A clerk received the message request and entered its route. The children ate bread from the ordinary emergency meal provision while their duck inspected the shelter floor. The elderly man said ducks always survived disasters better than people because they wasted no time explaining them. Wu laughed before realizing she had been ready to cry.

harbor_p09_006.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_006.text: The second crossing brought six more passengers. One carried a roll of cloth longer than the receiving bench. The crew had secured it as baggage within the permitted load and asked him to keep it clear of other people while disembarking. He claimed the cloth was more valuable than the barge. An attendant said then he should stop dragging it through a puddle. He lifted it at once. Yue saw the man's daughter hide a smile behind her hand. The landing had begun sounding like an ordinary place again, even while eleven people still remained aboard.

harbor_p09_007.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_007.text: On the third approach, the rescue pilot stopped short of the agreed position. A broken mooring stake had drifted into the gap between boat and barge. Yan kept the next passenger group behind the rail while the ordinary crew cleared it from the safe side with a boat hook. The delay frightened those waiting on shore because the craft looked motionless in the current. A runner supplied the actual reason and expected next check. Yue repeated that status only when asked. She did not turn a distant shape into a claim that the rescue had failed.

harbor_p09_008.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_008.text: The third group of six reached the shelter after the obstruction cleared and the pilot approved the approach again. Eighteen people were now ashore. The barge master and four other crew remained for the final crossing; the sixth crew member had traveled earlier with a passenger who needed help. The shore keeper checked actual arrivals against the master's reported total and the boat's transfer record. Names could be clarified later where spelling differed. Counting living people did not wait for every letter to match a contract. Five still remained, and the final boat went back for them.

harbor_p09_009.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_009.text: The final crossing carried the master and four barge crew, the rescue boat's two operators, and Yan in its eighth rated place. The receiving keeper reconciled the foreman's movement separately from the barge's twenty-three people. The vessel stayed grounded under the harbor master's direction. Saving everyone did not recover cargo or authorize people to go back aboard for belongings. The pilot closed the passenger rescue count at twenty-three safely landed, while the attendants turned to each person's immediate needs. Yan helped secure the craft before taking his own turn at the dry shelter.

harbor_p09_010.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_010.text: Yue noticed Yan's wet cuffs when he came to the dry shelter. He looked at the duck, which had escaped its basket and was investigating a discarded crust. He asked whose crew member it was. Wu Lian said it had no license and therefore expected preferential treatment. The foreman laughed, then sat for the first time since the boat left. He had no injury beyond an ordinary scraped knuckle, which the attendant cleaned after he agreed. Yue offered water. The task had ended successfully without giving him authority over the people he helped bring ashore.

harbor_p09_011.speaker: harbor_yan_su
harbor_p09_011.text: The boat did its rated work, the pilot stopped when the gap changed, and people listened even while frightened. That is the account I want the shore desk to keep. We do not need a tale where somebody ignored every limit and made the river admire him. We also need to know who still wants an urgent message sent and who needs ordinary care before another question. I can help with the equipment return after rest. I cannot tell Wu Lian where her family should stay, and I doubt the duck would accept my recommendation anyway.

harbor_p09_012.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_012.text: The barge crew worked for a transport contractor from another district. Their wages were not covered by the Salt Lantern guarantee. The desk could receive questions, preserve documents with permission, and refer the contract dispute. It could not pay them from a deposit that no longer existed. The master supplied a crew list and employer contact. Some workers feared that leaving the grounded vessel would be called abandoning work. Yan's rescue record showed the ordinary safety direction under which they left. The wage adviser would explain how that record could support their response without promising a decision outside harbor authority.

harbor_p09_013.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_013.text: One crew worker, Shui Rong, had packed at Old Salt Yard before taking the creek job. She recognized He Ming, who arrived with privately bought fruit for the waiting families. They embraced hard enough to bruise a pear. Shui was among the five people still owed a two-copper permit refund. Her old address had become obsolete when she traveled for work. He Ming told her which keeper held the claim and offered to walk there later. The immediate landing desk asked first whether she needed rest. The refund would remain hers if she did not collect it today.

harbor_p09_014.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_014.text: Shui Rong wanted only a dry place to change socks before any office visit. She had been aboard the barge for three days and had expected another morning of ordinary work, not a rescue. Her employer's agent would reach the harbor tomorrow. She did not want He Ming to speak for her employment claim. She would welcome help reading the public referral. He Ming listened to the difference and said she could do that. Yue watched the woman keep companionship available without turning recognition into a representative appointment neither had asked for.

harbor_p09_015.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_015.text: The cloth merchant's daughter was named Shan Aning. She had come to study accounts with an aunt who rented a market stall. Her father insisted she needed to help recover the cargo first. Aning said he could hire handling help after the harbor master decided whether recovery was safe. He accused her of enjoying his loss. The girl reddened and went quiet. Yue remained at the contact table rather than intervene as a family judge. When Aning asked to send a message to her aunt herself, the ordinary clerk received it under her own consent.

harbor_p09_016.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_016.text: The grounded barge's cargo included cloth, dried vegetables, tools and household bundles. Sui Yan's office checked the master's hazard account and asked for a technical inspection before handling. No report yet identified a contagious illness or dangerous residue. The captain would not issue a cargo quarantine merely because people looked frightened and muddy. Vessel stability and ordinary recovery belonged to the relevant harbor crews and keeper. Yue liked the precision but said nothing about it. The waiting passengers mainly wanted to know whether they could retrieve warm coats, not admire which license answered which question.

harbor_p09_017.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_017.text: Wu Lian's sister arrived after her packing shift with a borrowed handcart. She hugged the children before asking about the duck. The younger one explained its entire rescue in a breathless speech that left the mother looking exhausted. The sister could take the family for one night in her rented room if the landlord agreed to the actual number. Wu accepted the offer provisionally and asked to discuss longer arrangements tomorrow. An attendant supplied the current shelter option if that plan failed. Neither sister wanted emergency welcome to become a promise the crowded room could not keep.

harbor_p09_018.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_018.text: The cloth merchant found no immediate space at his preferred inn. He blamed the receiving clerk until Aning showed him the public list of other rooms. A plain lodge had two beds available at a rate he could afford. He refused because its roof looked patched. Aning asked whether the roof had leaked during the morning rain. The keeper said no and offered inspection before payment. They went to see it. Yue could not know what they decided afterward. Her inquiry page recorded the offered route and chosen contact request, leaving their ordinary lodging bargain to them.

harbor_p09_019.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_019.text: A passenger named Qiao Bensheng said he would remain in the landing shelter until his nephew came. The nephew's collection point lay inland, and a message could not reach him before evening. The shelter attendants explained the authorized overnight terms and meal arrangement without calling it detention. Qiao could leave if he chose another safe place. He said he liked a bench with people nearby. Yue asked whether his message could say that. He agreed and added that his nephew should bring the blanket with the red patch, because every other blanket in the house belonged to somebody else's complaint.

harbor_p09_020.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_020.text: By late afternoon, the care attendant had referred two people for further examination and cleared others to make their own lodging choices. The duck returned to its basket with a crust it stole from no identifiable claimant. Yue's half-day ended before the desk finished every family question. She handed the remaining requests to the assigned clerk with dates and sources visible. Her appointment did not stretch because the scene remained moving. He Ming stayed to accompany Shui after rest. Yan went to equipment return through port duty. The harbor continued its work with other people named to do it.

harbor_p09_021.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_021.text: Yue walked back to the repair shed and found herself hungry enough to resent every smell from a cooking stall. She bought a bowl with her own money and ate standing beneath an awning. The seller asked whether she had rescued the barge. She said the licensed boat and crew had, while she worked at the receiving table. He nodded and called her the rescue clerk anyway. She lacked the energy to correct him a second time. A story could acquire a false center through harmless conversation as easily as a dispatch packet acquired a missing leaf.

harbor_p09_022.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_022.text: At the shed, the boy wanted to know whether the duck used qi to escape. Yue said it used a poorly tied basket. He demanded to see the knot. She had not kept it, which he found an unreasonable failure in an otherwise promising account. Han Pei arrived with the office's ordinary completion notice and laughed at his disappointment. The duck had no registered powers. Its survival remained an excellent story. They agreed on that without turning the animal into another creature Yue needed to bind, carry, feed or explain before leaving the harbor.

harbor_p09_023.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_023.text: Han said the new arrivals exposed a problem the wage correction did not solve. The public instructions told people which office handled questions, but tired people reached several questions at once. Yue described Wu Lian asking for a message before agreeing where to sleep. Han wrote that example with the woman's permission for feedback, omitting private contact details. Their proposed help route should begin with what the person needed now, then assign the next question without making the whole life fit one form. The thought seemed obvious until they tried to put actual staffing beside it.

harbor_p09_024.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_024.text: The next morning, Shui Rong collected her two-copper refund after the permit keeper verified her identity and original charge reference. The actual paid total rose from forty-eight to fifty, leaving eight held for four identified payers. She chose not to combine it with her new barge wage question. The refund concerned an old yard charge; her current contractor owed whatever its own contract established. He Ming watched the keeper show both references separately. Shui said keeping money distinct was easier than keeping employers distinct, because foremen tended to make the same face when asked for a calculation.

harbor_p09_025.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_025.text: The contractor's agent arrived at the landing shelter carrying a wet satchel and a bad temper. He wanted the barge crew to report immediately for salvage preparations. The harbor master had not yet approved boarding or recovery. Yan Su, present through ordinary duty, showed the relevant hold direction and asked for tasks workers could safely do ashore. The agent said waiting cost him money. Shui asked whether he intended to pay their contracted time. He had brought no calculation. The wage adviser received that question and asked him to supply the contract and proposed assignments in writing.

harbor_p09_026.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_026.text: Shui's friend, a young crewman named Luo Tai, wanted to agree to anything that kept another voyage available. He had a parent relying on remittances inland. Shui said her own family needed money too, and a grounded barge would not become stable because they were afraid of a foreman. The argument took place beside the ordinary job board, where other waiting people listened. Yue did not call one brave and the other weak. Each had pressure the hearing forms would need to understand without allowing that pressure to authorize an unsafe return.

harbor_p09_027.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_027.text: The agent offered a paid shore inventory task while the vessel decision proceeded. The contract required confirmation of rate and hours, which the wage adviser helped make explicit within the relevant rules. Shui accepted after reading the terms. Luo Tai accepted too and looked relieved enough to pretend he had never worried. Their work began at a dry table using cargo references brought ashore by the master, not inside the grounded hold. Safe alternative employment did not resolve every wage question. It gave the day a task that did not require a worker to pretend the river was harmless.

harbor_p09_028.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_028.text: Wu Lian returned to the shelter desk because her sister's landlord allowed one night but refused a longer stay at that occupancy. The landlord supplied the room rule; the sisters did not have a contract for more. An ordinary housing adviser showed temporary options and their actual rates. Wu had brought savings for travel and work search, not enough to rent a family room indefinitely. She wanted to find paid work before taking another journey. Yue could help read the public options during her second scheduled inquiry shift, while the adviser held the housing task after that shift ended.

harbor_p09_029.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_029.text: The children argued about whether the duck deserved a separate bed. Their aunt said it deserved to stay outside, where ordinary ducks belonged. The younger one called that exile. Wu laughed and then apologized for laughing while she had no room. The housing adviser said the children could remain cheerful without making her need less real. That answer settled the woman more than a list of rates did. Yue wrote the family's chosen contact point into its own permission field, knowing a useful temporary address should not quietly become proof they had found a lasting home.

harbor_p09_030.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_030.text: Aning reached her aunt's market stall before her father completed the cargo visit he expected her to make. The aunt sold cloth and knew the father's business well enough to separate his worry from his instructions. She offered Aning a paid trial helping with accounts, with a bed at home for an agreed fortnight if the household arrangements suited. Aning asked to see the rate and tasks. Her aunt grinned and said the harbor had taught everybody to distrust generosity. The girl said generosity was fine; she wanted to know which part was work.

harbor_p09_031.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_031.text: Aning's father arrived at the aunt's stall and found his daughter checking a day's purchases. He demanded that she come help with the grounded cargo. Her aunt asked what permitted task he had assigned and whether it was paid. He said a daughter should not require wages to care about family loss. Aning said she cared and still wanted her study agreement honored. The aunt suggested a bounded unpaid family visit after the paid shift, if Aning chose it. Her father disliked being offered a choice where he expected obedience. He finally agreed to discuss it over supper.

harbor_p09_032.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_032.text: The discussion took place at the aunt's ordinary kitchen table. Yue did not attend. Aning later told the receiving clerk that she would remain at the aunt's chosen contact point and work the agreed trial. Her father would pursue cargo recovery through its proper route. The clerk recorded the current choice with permission, not the whole argument. Yue read the status during supervised comparison and was glad the family's public trail did not require a transcript of the private meal. Some useful outcomes deserved enough documentation to work and enough silence to leave people a life outside it.

harbor_p09_033.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_033.text: Qiao Bensheng's nephew arrived after dusk with the requested red-patched blanket. He had also brought the wrong pair of shoes. The older man complained as though the mistake proved affection had deteriorated with the younger generation. The nephew said he could leave the shoes if criticism needed to remain comfortable. They both laughed. The shelter keeper recorded the chosen departure after Qiao confirmed it himself. He would stay at the nephew's room for an agreed interval. Rescue had made no one the owner of his next decision, even when a younger relative came with a blanket and convincing concern.

harbor_p09_034.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_034.text: The next tide inspection showed the grounded barge could be stabilized for controlled recovery before a later repair move. The harbor master authorized only the specific crew plan approved by the maritime keeper. Passenger entry remained closed. The cloth merchant hired handling staff through the permitted operation rather than sending Aning aboard. His cargo references identified what could be brought to shore first. Several household bundles received priority because their owners needed coats and medicine containers, subject to the actual handling conditions. Sui's staff checked relevant hazard questions without making a dramatic quarantine story from ordinary wet cargo.

harbor_p09_035.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_035.text: The recovery crew found the barge's strike point against a submerged old stake. Its location differed from the current channel chart. The pilot supplied his route account, and the harbor keeper opened a navigation review. An old marker's existence did not prove the pilot ignored directions or the chart keeper concealed a danger. The broken wood and position were recorded before removal. Yan Su asked whether the replacement marking could be checked before another vessel passed. The relevant keeper arranged it through existing duties. Yue heard the public status while helping read a family-property collection form.

harbor_p09_036.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_036.text: Wu Lian's household bundles included a tin holding ordinary medicine prescribed for the elderly man traveling beside her, not for either child. The items had been placed together to protect them from water. The receiving clerk asked the man to confirm the collection authority and its limit. Wu did not own the tin because it sat in her blanket roll. The crew brought the cleared bundle through the recorded process, and the man collected his medicine container with an attendant's help. Wu's children were more interested in recovering a toy boat that had lost its sail during the crossing.

harbor_p09_037.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_037.text: The younger child wanted to float the toy from the quay steps immediately. Yan stopped him at the dry boundary and showed the ordinary square's shallow water basin instead. The child accused him of fearing boats. The foreman said he respected places where boats belonged and places children belonged, which were sometimes different. Wu laughed while securing the duck basket more carefully. Yue watched the boy launch his damaged toy in the basin and found its crooked progress oddly moving. A frightening morning could leave a child impatient for another small voyage before the adults felt ready to breathe.

harbor_p09_038.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_038.text: The housing adviser found Wu a two-week room offer above a net shed, with the actual family occupancy agreed and a safe stair inspected. The rate was within her immediate savings. It did not become subsidized forever because the family arrived through a rescue. A nearby canteen offered a paid kitchen trial that fitted the school hour her sister could help arrange. Wu inspected both before accepting. Yue joined only for the public-rate reading within her inquiry shift. She did not sign the lease for Wu or promise the canteen would keep her beyond its stated trial.

harbor_p09_039.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_039.text: He Ming visited the room privately with a pot and two cups she gave from her own household stores. Wu thanked her and said she had brought cups already. He Ming nearly insisted, then asked whether the pot was useful. It was. She took the cups home, amused and embarrassed. Helping had always felt easier when the needed thing was exactly what she offered. The woman who accepted one object and refused two made kindness less flattering and more practical. Yue heard the story over supper and admired He Ming for laughing at it without making Wu seem ungrateful.

harbor_p09_040.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_040.text: At the canteen trial, Wu learned the serving order faster than the owner expected and burnt the first tray of buns. The owner paid the agreed trial rate, explaining that the waste belonged to a training task she authorized. Wu wanted to reimburse flour from her savings. The owner declined and asked her to note the oven timing for the next attempt. Yue saw them through the open door while passing to the office. The second tray came out pale at one end and good enough to sell at the other. A job began through mistakes rather than rescue gratitude.

harbor_p09_041.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_041.text: Shui Rong's contractor submitted the crew calculation to the wage adviser. It identified worked shifts, paid advances, shore inventory hours and the disputed grounding interval. The adviser could explain the terms and preserve the crew's response, while the decision route belonged to the contract's competent office. Shui copied her own relevant lines and asked about two omitted hours. The agent found a shore tally that supported them and corrected his proposal. Luo Tai looked relieved, then ashamed he had almost accepted the first number without checking. Shui said fear could remain while a person asked an ordinary question.

harbor_p09_042.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_042.text: The contractor would pay the undisputed current amount through the agreed route without requiring withdrawal of the grounding-time question. The crew received that distinction in writing before deciding whether to accept new work. No Salt Lantern bond paid any part. Yue's task was to help the harbor contact pages reflect the crew members' chosen locations while they waited. Their employment adviser handled calculations. The separate assignments kept her appointment from turning into a job she never agreed to perform. Shui appreciated the division after learning who could answer the wage question without being sent through another chain of buildings.

harbor_p09_043.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_043.text: Luo Tai asked whether a cultivator could persuade the agent to stop retaliating if the crew disputed the interval. Yue said the labor route could receive an actual threat and preserve evidence; she had no power to guarantee the next hiring. He said her visible arms made people listen. She answered that fear of her would leave the question waiting when she departed. He looked dissatisfied, then took the report desk reference. The small answer felt inadequate to both of them. Its value lay in being one the harbor could still offer next month when Yue's pack had moved inland.

harbor_p09_044.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_044.text: That evening, He Ming found Yue at the shore wall and said the response desk seemed to end conversations where people still needed protection. Yue agreed that a named route was not enough unless it worked. They discussed the actual threat Luo Tai feared and what responsible staff could check without promising certainty. He Ming wanted the proposed continuation term to test that route in practice. Yue wanted the harbor to own the task rather than borrow her reputation. The two wishes met painfully. Both required paid people to answer when a powerful employer disliked the reply.

harbor_p09_045.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_045.text: Han Pei joined them with a roster draft for future contact work. The administrator had asked for costs and duties, not approved continuation yet. A clerk would hold responsibility for unanswered questions beyond Yue's shifts. Existing staff needed a realistic timetable so ordinary queues did not disappear while outreach improved. He Ming asked whether Han would be that clerk. Han said only if the assignment and hours fitted her workload. Yue liked hearing her say it. The gull had taught the wage clerk no law, but it seemed to have improved her refusal to treat every need as hers alone.

harbor_p09_046.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_046.text: The three women ate at a stall whose cook put too much vinegar into the first bowl. He Ming argued, Han quietly moved hers aside, and Yue ate it before deciding the problem was real. The cook offered a corrected portion after tasting the pot. Their different approaches made them laugh. He Ming said Yue sometimes tried to endure uncertainty until it became a meal. Yue admitted she had once considered vinegar an invitation to demonstrate patience. Han said that would be a useless doctrine, and ordered fresh rice. Friendship could correct ordinary judgment more pleasantly than a hearing did.

harbor_p09_047.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_047.text: Aning completed her aunt's paid trial and chose another fortnight. Her father accepted the cargo recovery schedule and rented safe storage for cleared cloth through his own account. He still wanted her help after hours, but began asking which evening rather than summoning her at any moment. The aunt insisted family work should have an end too. Aning wrote that agreement into her personal calendar, not a harbor contract. Yue saw her laughing with Fen at the binder's stall. Two young women who arrived through different losses had found a shared impatience with adults calling every choice a lesson.

harbor_p09_048.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_048.text: Fen showed Aning the fish kite, which had acquired so many repairs that its first paper was mostly memory. Aning suggested a stronger tail fabric from an ordinary offcut her father authorized her to give. The boy accepted the scrap as a gift and wanted to paint a market stall onto the fish's back. They negotiated its weight for an entire afternoon. Yue watched from the stair while sewing her pack strap. The kite would remain here after she left. That thought made the noisy argument feel precious enough that she did not offer an efficient way to settle it.

harbor_p09_049.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_049.text: Luo Jian received his month's paper-sorting wages for completed shifts and checked the payment against the agreed rate. He set aside rent and care travel before buying a new cup for the binder's shop. His old chipped cup stayed at home because it belonged to a private story. Fen said purchased cups might improve the shop's professional appearance more than his handwriting. He told her the handwriting survived enough hiring desks to deserve respect. They ate supper on wages earned in jobs neither expected when the Salt Lantern first arrived. The change was modest and large at the same time.

harbor_p09_050.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_050.text: Dai Min sold another net and put the payment into her own purse. A customer asked whether she would return to Willow Reach when the harbor work slowed. She said she had not decided. The question annoyed her because people seemed to expect grief to provide an itinerary. He Ming agreed to discuss work opportunities instead of asking what home now meant. Yue listened at their table and recognized the same pressure in a kinder form. Others wanted a person's next journey to explain the past. Sometimes the journey needed only a bed, a rate, and a choice still open.

harbor_p09_051.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_051.text: The permit keeper reached two refund payers through existing scheduled collection routes. They verified identity and authority, and four copper was delivered with acknowledged receipts. The separate refund account had now paid fifty-four to twenty-seven of the twenty-nine people, leaving four for two recipients still under contact review. Shui's two had been included earlier in that fifty-four. The keeper's public aggregate stated both completion and hold. Yue checked it before linking feedback into the proposed term report. Tiny sums deserved exact counts because the office could otherwise call a nearly complete remedy complete and leave the last people invisible again.

harbor_p09_052.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_052.text: The two unresolved refund entries belonged to workers whose old contact points had closed. No evidence showed they refused payment. The permit office asked the relevant destination keeper for safe contact through its ordinary process. Yue would not carry a rumor through every lodging house on her free time to make the table look finished. She could use one remaining scheduled outreach task if it helped the households already linked to her appointment. Han kept the review date visible. The four copper stayed earmarked, giving the unknown a concrete duty instead of allowing it to disappear beneath an encouraging percentage.

harbor_p09_053.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_053.text: Sui Yan inspected the recovered cargo's relevant handling notes and found no reason for a new quarantine order. The grounded barge still required maritime repair approval, and several wet food lots needed ordinary condition review before sale. She issued the narrow technical status and went to the canteen where Wu Lian now worked. The woman served her a bun that had risen beautifully and leaned sideways. Sui said it resembled half the harbor's committees. Wu laughed and charged the posted price. The captain could eat among arrivals without becoming the owner of every answer they needed.

harbor_p09_054.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_054.text: Yan Su finished the barge rescue equipment return under the maintenance record. Rated lines and slings went back for inspection and drying. The boat crew recorded four loaded crossings and twenty-three barge people ashore, plus their own personnel movements. Yue checked the public aggregate against the receiving register; she did not certify nautical work. The account explicitly placed Yan in the final eighth rated seat, outside the rescued-vessel count. The correct detail prevented a story about twenty-four passengers from growing out of the familiar foreman standing beside those he helped. He appreciated the accuracy and disliked being counted so publicly.

harbor_p09_055.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_055.text: Bo claimed the duck should make the official total twenty-four. The desk said passenger counts covered people and kept baggage separately. The boy at the shed disagreed, arguing the duck displayed more personality than several adults. Yan refused to reopen a completed rescue register for philosophical poultry. Yue laughed while Han explained that baggage was no insult to the animal. It merely had a different line. The argument followed them into supper until Wu's child announced the duck had laid an egg. That actual new contribution ended the count dispute more decisively than any form instruction could have done.

harbor_p09_056.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_056.text: On the eleventh week's last paid inquiry half-day, Yue completed the new-arrival contact comparison and handed ongoing tasks to the assigned desk. Twenty-two of her twenty-four shifts were complete, with forty-four of forty-eight wages earned. Expenses remained ten copying, twelve interpretation and six ferry. No extra qi had been used during the grounded-barge rescue or receiving work. Her established fourth-stage practice continued only in rest intervals. She wrote the two remaining shifts in the next week's calendar and listed tasks that could fit them. The harbor's next needs would not silently acquire her time by appearing before that calendar ended.

harbor_p09_057.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_057.text: The administrator invited Yue, Han, He Ming and the relevant staff to a proposal meeting before the term closure. A possible fourteen-week continuation would use a separately authorized operations allocation, not claimant funds. It remained a draft until duties and costs were agreed. Yue said she would consider a real offer, not a moral appointment to stay wherever work existed. He Ming looked hurt before recognizing that she wanted the same right for the arrivals she helped. The woman nodded. Their friendship could ask Yue to remain; it could not make a departure proof she cared less than promised.

harbor_p09_058.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_058.text: Yue opened her travel notes that night and looked at roads beyond the harbor. No kiln employer had written offering a post. She had heard of inland workshops through ordinary travelers, and could investigate when she chose to leave. Her habitual pack still held the same bedding, cup, blade, practice notes and wrapped pendant. Harbor loan boards stayed at the office. She added nothing from the rescue stores to make a future story more convenient. The possible continuation would be work she chose on its own terms. She closed the map without needing the roads to feel abandoned.

harbor_p09_059.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_059.text: Han came to the shed after her painting lesson and found Yue with the closed map. She asked whether she wanted help comparing the draft terms or simply company. Yue chose company first. They sat while the boy painted Aning's fabric scrap the wrong color and insisted it was artistic judgment. Han did not correct the brush stroke until he asked. Yue appreciated the restraint. She had spent weeks helping people ask a usable question. At home, friendship could begin by offering choices and survive an answer that required doing nothing immediately useful.

harbor_p09_060.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_060.text: He Ming wrote to Mother that the room's plant survived, the barge people landed safely, and the harbor might keep Yue for another term. She crossed out keep and wrote hire if she wished. The change pleased her enough to show Han the next morning. The clerk laughed and asked whether the plant had agreed to its lodging. He Ming said it had lodged a protest through one dead leaf. Their jokes had grown a language of their own. Yue hoped the women would continue it after she left, though she knew she could neither require nor document that future.

harbor_p09_061.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_061.text: The grounded barge moved under approved maritime conditions to a repair position after its recovery work completed. Its master retained responsibility for repair and employer records. The shore families made separate decisions: Qiao stayed with his nephew, Wu began the canteen term and temporary family room, Aning remained at her aunt's trial work. The crew's undisputed wages followed their contract route while the disputed interval remained under review. The public completion account said what actually closed and what did not. Yue liked the several endings because no single happy household scene had to carry every person's arrival.

harbor_p09_062.speaker: narrator
harbor_p09_062.text: The twelfth-week notice on Yue's appointment appeared in the office roster. Han had written its end date from the beginning and now treated that date as real. They would close shifts, expenses, lodging charges and borrowed materials before any new agreement. Yue felt gratitude for the formal ending. It gave her room to decide whether another beginning was wanted. He Ming brought breakfast to the desk privately and asked what the last two shifts needed. The women named achievable tasks instead of everything still wrong with the harbor. For once, the list's shortness sounded like respect rather than neglect.
